Topic 01 — Youth Populations & LTAD

Four Concepts to Know First

1
Athleticism
Motor competency + balance, strength, power, speed, agility, endurance
2
LTAD
Long-term athletic development — athleticism built progressively over years
3
YPD Model
Lloyd & Oliver's youth physical development framework
4
Trainability
Children's responsiveness to the resistance training stimulus
Topic 01 — Core Definition

What Is Athleticism?

Athleticism

Ability to repeatedly execute varied movements with precision & confidence, across environments. Requires motor skill competency, balance, coordination, strength, power, speed, agility, endurance.

Not reserved for competitive athletes — a goal for everyone.

NSCA View — LTAD develops athleticism over time to boost fitness, cut injury risk, improve physical & mental health. Relevant at all ages, but critical focus for youth over past two decades.

Topic 01 — Common Ground Across Models

What All LTAD Models Agree On

01 — Broad Exposure
Children exposed to wide range of activities targeting motor skill development & muscular strength.
02 — Simple → Advanced
Training starts simple, becomes more advanced as children progress through developmental stages.
03 — Generic → Specific
Generic training early on; specialization increases as workload & training exposure grow.
Bespoke models exist for agility, speed, power, endurance, motor skills, resistance training, plyometrics & weightlifting — but they converge on these three principles.
Topic 01 — The Evidence Base

RT Effectiveness Is Unequivocal

  • 01
    Leading international consensus statements confirm RT enhances multiple fitness components in youth.
  • 02
    Seminal meta-analytical data supports effectiveness across children & adolescents.
  • 03
    Youth sports training has grown more intense & complex — raising injury-risk factors that must be considered alongside benefits.
  • 04
    S&C professionals must understand how growth, maturation & development affect adaptations and confound testing data.
Key Takeaway — Topic 01

LTAD Is a Lifelong Lens

Athletic development isn't reserved for competitive sport outcomes. Every child benefits from a long-term, well-rounded approach that builds motor skill competency and muscular strength side by side.

Topic 02

The
Growing
Child

Growth, development & maturation — three related but distinct processes

Topic 02 — The Growing Child

Three Terms, Three Meanings

1
Growth
Increase in body size, or a particular body part
2
Development
Natural progression from prenatal life to adulthood
3
Maturation
Progress toward a fully mature state; timing, tempo, magnitude vary by system
Puberty — the period when secondary sex characteristics develop and a child transitions toward young adulthood. Body composition & physical skill performance change markedly, and vary widely between individuals.
Topic 02 — Chronological vs Biological

Age on the Calendar Isn't Age in the Body

A group of 14-year-olds can differ in height by up to 9 inches (23 cm) and in weight by up to 40 lb (18 kg). An 11-year-old girl may be taller & more skilled than an 11-year-old boy.

Puberty onset ranges 8-13 years in girls, 9-15 in boys — girls begin roughly two years before boys.

Biological maturation — measured via skeletal age, sexual maturation, or somatic (physique) maturation. Skeletal age (X-ray of wrist) is gold standard but impractical for most practitioners.
"Two children of the same chronological age can differ biologically by up to five years."
Ref: Figure 7.2 — Essentials of Strength Training & Conditioning, 5th Ed. (NSCA)
Topic 02 — Bone Growth (Figure 7.2)
From Fetus to Fused Bone

Most bone formation occurs in the diaphysis (shaft) and growth cartilage at the epiphyseal plate, joint surface & apophyseal insertions.

  • 01
    Diaphysis — the central shaft where most bone forms via the primary ossification center.
  • 02
    Growth cartilage — secondary ossification center; when the epiphyseal plate fully ossifies, long bones stop growing.
Topic 02 — Muscle & Strength Growth

"Stretch Out Before They Fill Out"

Muscle Mass
25% of body weight at birth → ~40% by adulthood. Growth via fiber hypertrophy, not hyperplasia.
Peak Strength Timing
Boys: ~1.2 yrs after PHV, 0.8 yrs after peak weight velocity. Girls: after PHV too, with more individual variation.
Peak Muscle Mass
16-20 yrs in females; 18-25 yrs in males — unless altered by exercise or diet.
Adolescents show absolute strength gains ~50% greater than children (meta-analytic data). Boys accelerate post-puberty due to hormones; girls typically plateau.
Topic 02 — Individualizing the Program

Technical Competency, Training Age & Skill Literacy

  • 01
    Technical competency — how well the child moves.
  • 02
    Training age — length of time following a formalized, supervised RT program.
  • 03
    RT skill literacy — how children think, connect & feel about resistance training.
A 13-year-old early-maturing, experienced girl may handle advanced training; a 16-year-old late-maturing, untrained boy may need introductory approaches — chronological age alone doesn't decide readiness.
Topic 02 — Anthropometric Variation

Body Proportions Change the Lift

Short Arms + Large Chest
Biomechanical advantage in upper-body pressing exercises.
Long Legs + Long Torso
Biomechanical disadvantage in squatting movements.
Practical Fix
Use child-size machines or body weight / medicine balls / bands / dumbbells / barbells. With low coach-to-athlete ratios, individualize 1-2 exercises per session using simple field-test results.
Key Takeaway — Topic 02

Biology, Not the Calendar, Leads

Two children of the same chronological age can differ biologically by up to five years. Program design must account for maturation, technical competency & training age — not just the birth certificate.

Topic 03

Youth
Resistance
Training

Safe, effective, and misunderstood — what the evidence actually shows

Topic 03 — Safety Consensus

Children Are Not Miniature Adults

Clinicians, coaches & exercise scientists agree: resistance exercise is a safe, effective conditioning method for children, provided programs are appropriately designed & supervised.

WHO recommends muscle- & bone-strengthening activity 3 times/week as part of youth physical activity guidelines.

Golden rule — underestimate physical abilities and progress volume/intensity gradually. Adult training philosophies (and their intensity/volume) should never be superimposed on youth.
Topic 03 — Responsiveness to Training

Yes, Children Are Trainable

  • 01
    Early "no effect" studies suffered short duration / low volume-intensity — not proof RT doesn't work.
  • 02
    Strength gains of 30-40% typical in untrained preadolescents after 8-20 week programs.
  • 03
    Gains are larger with programs >23 weeks and intensities >80% 1RM.
  • 04
    Children as young as age 5 benefit from developmentally appropriate RT.
Topic 03 — Detraining & Long-Term Gains

What Happens When Training Stops (or Continues)

Detraining
Strength gains are impermanent — tend to return toward untrained control values once training stops. PE/sport alone won't maintain them.
1x vs 2x /Week
Training once weekly produced only 67% of the strength gains of twice-weekly training.
2-Year Study
German youth soccer players (11-19y) on linear periodized RT made substantial gains in squat strength, speed & change-of-direction.
Ref: Figure 7.3 — Adapted from Faigenbaum, Lloyd & Myer, Essentials of Strength Training & Conditioning, 5th Ed. (NSCA)
Topic 03 — Mechanism of Strength Gains (Figure 7.3)
Neural First, Hypertrophy Later

Preadolescent strength gains come mainly from neural factors (motor unit activation/synchronization) — testosterone in preadolescents is only 20-60 ng/100mL, rising to ~600 ng/100mL in adolescent males.

  • ●
    Neural myelination development — drives early gains via motor development.
  • ●
    Theoretical fiber type differentiation — contributes progressively through preadolescence.
  • ●
    Androgenic hormones — stay low, then climb sharply into adolescence.
  • ●
    Lean body mass — consolidates alongside hormonal changes at adolescence.
Topic 03 — Myths vs Facts

Dispelling the Myths of Youth RT

Myth vs Fact
"Resistance training stunts bone growth."
False —RT stimulates bone remodeling & strengthens bone, muscle & connective tissue.
"It's unsafe for children."
False —With correct technique, loading & instruction, RT is safe for all youth.
"Only for young athletes."
False —Benefits all youth, competitive or not.
"Kids will get 'bulky'."
False —Childhood RT drives neuromuscular adaptation; girls in particular see lower absolute muscle growth due to lower androgens.
Topic 03 — Injury Risk

The Weight Room Is Safer Than the Field

Joint forces during sport participation are often greater and less predictable than those in a supervised resistance training program.

Injuries in the weight room are more likely accidental, typically linked to inadequate supervision, poor technical competency, or inappropriate loads.

Epiphyseal fractures — reported cases were case studies, typically heavy overhead lifts in unsupervised settings. Not reported in any prospective, guideline-adherent youth RT study.
Key Takeaway — Topic 03

The Evidence Is Unequivocal

Properly programmed resistance training is safe and effective for children and adolescents. The myths persist — the data does not support them.

Topic 04

Program
Design for
Children

From needs analysis to athletic motor skill competencies

Topic 04 — Where Design Begins

Needs Analysis First

No minimum age for RT participation — but the child needs the emotional maturity to receive/follow directions and want to try.

A needs analysis assesses the individual's physical, technical & psychosocial characteristics against the demands of their sport or activity.

Goals extend beyond strength: teaching body awareness, promoting interest in activity, weight-room etiquette, and fun. A pretraining medical exam isn't mandatory for healthy children, but injury/illness screening is essential.
Topic 04 — Athletic Motor Skill Competencies (Figure 7.4)

The AMSC Spectrum

Eight AMSC domains represent the foundational movements underpinning all athletic movement. Programs should develop form (technique) and function (force production) across them over time — not necessarily all in one session.
Topic 04 — Assessing Strength Safely

Testing Without Excess Risk

1RM & Isometric
Proven safe in youth when appropriate warm-up, progression & supervision are followed.
Predictive Equations
5RM/10RM estimates avoid true 1RM, but repeated reps risk cumulative fatigue affecting technical form.
Field-Based Alternatives
Vertical/long jump & handgrip strength correlate significantly with 1RM in youth — a practical surrogate.
Whichever protocol is used, the child must demonstrate & maintain correct technique throughout, under the watchful eye of a qualified professional.
Topic 04 — Youth RT Guidelines

The Non-Negotiables

  • ✓Each child understands the benefits & risks of resistance training.
  • ✓Sessions designed & supervised by competent professionals, considering growth & maturation.
  • ✓Environment safe, hazard-free; equipment sized to fit each child.
  • ✓Dynamic warm-up & exploratory play before training; static stretching after, when appropriate.
  • ✓Begin with light loads; increase resistance gradually (5-10%) as technique & strength improve.
  • ✓2-3 nonconsecutive sessions/week — more frequent for higher training-age youth.
  • ✓Advanced lifts (snatch, clean & jerk) permitted once technical proficiency is prioritized.
Key Takeaway — Topic 04

Technique Over Load, Always

Training intensity should never be increased at the expense of technical competency or psychosocial maturity. Individualize through variation — technical difficulty, range of motion, movement speed — not just weight.

Aging:
MSK &
Neuromuscular
Health

Bone, muscle & nervous system changes that drive falls and functional decline

Topic 05 — Age-Related Changes

Four Conditions to Know

1
Osteopenia
Bone mineral density -1 to -2.5 SD below young adult mean
2
Osteoporosis
Bone mineral density below -2.5 SD — heightened fracture risk
3
Sarcopenia
Progressive skeletal muscle disorder — falls, fractures, disability, mortality risk
4
Dynapenia
Age-related loss of muscle strength/power, distinct from muscle mass loss
Ref: Figure 7.5 — © Paul Gunning / Science Source, via Essentials of Strength Training & Conditioning, 5th Ed. (NSCA)
Topic 05 — Bone Structure (Figure 7.5)
Healthy Bone vs Osteoporotic Bone

Osteopenia/osteoporosis develop as bone mineral content decreases and porosity increases, raising fracture risk at hip, spine, or wrist during a fall.

(A) Healthy Bone
Dense, tightly packed trabecular struts with small pore spaces.
(B) Osteoporotic Bone
Thinner struts, larger pore spaces — reduced density and structural strength.

Topic 05 — Neuromuscular Function & Falls

Why Seniors Fall

Intrinsic fall-risk factors: decrements in muscle strength/power, slower reaction time, impaired balance & postural stability.

Preactivation (before ground contact) and cocontraction (agonist + antagonist together) help stabilize joints — but cocontraction reduces net force output.

Seniors rely on increased cocontraction to compensate for balance difficulty & minimize postural sway — a trade-off between stability and force production.
Topic 05 — Power Loss & Function

Power Recedes Faster Than Strength

  • 01
    Decreased muscle mass → loss of strength; gradual denervation of muscle fibers reduces power (force production speed) even faster.
  • 02
    40% of women 55-64y, 45% of 65-74y, 65% of 75-84y couldn't lift 10 lb (4.5 kg).
  • 03
    Reduced mechanical power during gait push-off is a key biomechanical aging feature.
  • 04
    Everyday tasks — stair climbing, rising from a chair — depend on rapid force production, not just maximal strength.
Key Takeaway — Topic 05

Inactivity Is the Real Driver

Advancing age is linked to loss of muscle power, strength & mass — but this is largely attributable to physical inactivity, not aging alone. The result: decreased functional independence and increased fall/fracture risk.

Topic 06

Resistance
Training for
Older Adults

Reversing decline, rebuilding confidence, and preserving independence

Topic 06 — Responsiveness

Trainable at Any Age

  • 01
    Sedentary older men more than doubled knee extensor strength & tripled knee flexor strength after 12 weeks of RT.
  • 02
    Very old men & women (87-96 years) improved strength after just 8 weeks of RT.
  • 03
    Meta-analytic data: 800+ seniors aged 75-97 showed significant strength & whole-muscle hypertrophy gains.
  • 04
    A dose-response relationship exists — higher-intensity RT builds more maximal strength than moderate/low intensity.
Topic 06 — Power vs Traditional RT

Speed of Force Matters Too

High-Velocity Power Training
Greater gains in peak power vs slow-velocity RT, with similar maximal strength gains (Fielding et al., 16-week study).
Traditional Progressive RT
Effective for maximal strength; can be equally effective as power training for functional muscle architecture & activation in some outcomes.
Declines in muscle power are associated with disability & ability to perform ADLs — particularly in females. Minimizing age-related power deficits is a key exercise prescription goal.
Topic 06 — Bone Health

Building & Losing Bone Density

Meta-analytic data (1,130 participants, mean age ~70): progressive RT significantly increased strength and BMD of femur/hip — favoring lower volumes with higher external loads.

≥ 2 sessions/week of high-velocity RT can significantly raise BMD.

But it's reversible — skeletal adaptations can be lost when training stops for >6 months. Bone density tends to revert toward preexercise levels during inactivity.
Topic 06 — Myths vs Facts

Dispelling the Fears of RT for Seniors

Myth vs Fact
"RT will injure the musculoskeletal system."
False —Technique-focused, individualized, qualified-professional-led RT is safe and promotes positive bone/muscle adaptation.
"Unsafe with CV or MSK contraindications."
False —RT can be modified — lower volume/intensity, avoid Valsalva, simplify variants.
"RT takes too much time."
False —Meaningful gains from minimal-dose programs (≤60 min, 2x/week); "exercise snacking" (<10 min bouts) also works.
"Requires a fitness center."
False —Home-based resistance exercise can produce meaningful adaptation, though supervised training is preferable.
Topic 06 — Safety Recommendations

The Non-Negotiables

  • ✓Prescreen participants — many seniors have age-related medical conditions; seek medical advice where needed.
  • ✓Warm up 5-10 minutes: low-to-moderate aerobic activity + calisthenics.
  • ✓Static stretching before and/or after each session.
  • ✓Use resistance that does not excessively overload the musculoskeletal system.
  • ✓Avoid the Valsalva maneuver — it raises blood pressure abruptly.
  • ✓Allow 48-72 hours recovery between sessions.
  • ✓Perform all exercises within a pain-free range of motion.
Topic 06 — Program Progression

From Cautious Start to Confident Load

Early Phase
40-50% 1RM
1 set × 8-12 reps
Progression
60-80% 1RM
2-3 sets × 6-12 reps
Consensus Target
70-85% 1RM
2-3 sets, 2-3x/week
Power Add-On
40-60% 1RM
1-3 sets × 6-10, high velocity
Early stage priorities: education, reducing anxiety, building confidence — not maximal loading.
Key Takeaway — Topic 06

A Lifelong Commitment

Older men and women can make significant strength, power, mobility & functional gains through periodized RT — but bone and neuromuscular benefits are retained only as long as training continues.

Chapter 07 — Recap

Age-Related Differences at a Glance

✓Youth & LTADAthleticism is a lifelong goal built through progressive, well-rounded training.
✓The Growing ChildBiological maturation, not chronological age, should guide program design.
✓Youth RTSafe & effective when supervised, progressive & technique-focused.
✓Program DesignNeeds analysis + AMSC framework guide individualized youth programming.
✓Aging MSK/NM HealthSarcopenia, dynapenia & falls risk are largely driven by inactivity.
✓RT for Older AdultsTrainable at any age — benefits require a lifelong training commitment.
